claims.evidence: This is supported by ThT assays and TEM data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Structure-based peptide inhibitors reduce toxicity of already-aggregated Aβ species.
claims.source: Using this structure, we designed peptide-based inhibitors that reduce Aβ aggregation and toxicity of already-aggregated species.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT toxicity assays shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The designed inhibitors reduce the efficiency of Aβ-mediated tau aggregation.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, we also found that these inhibitors reduce the efficiency of Aβ-mediated tau aggregation, and moreover reduce aggregation and self-seeding of tau fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is supported by biosensor cell assays shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The designed inhibitors reduce aggregation and self-seeding of tau fibrils.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, we also found that these inhibitors reduce the efficiency of Aβ-mediated tau aggregation, and moreover reduce aggregation and self-seeding of tau fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ThT assays and biosensor cell experiments shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Aβ and tau fibrils share a common epitope.
claims.source: The ability of these inhibitors to interfere with both Aβ and tau seeds suggests these fibrils share a common epitope, and supports the hypothesis that cross-seeding is one mechanism by which amyloid is linked to tau aggregation and could promote cognitive decline.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the dual efficacy of the inhibitors against both proteins.

claims.claim: Cross-seeding is one mechanism by which amyloid is linked to tau aggregation.
claims.source: The ability of these inhibitors to interfere with both Aβ and tau seeds suggests these fibrils share a common epitope, and supports the hypothesis that cross-seeding is one mechanism by which amyloid is linked to tau aggregation and could promote cognitive decline.
claims.evidence: This hypothesis is supported by the experimental data showing Aβ can seed tau aggregation.

claims.claim: Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent form of dementia.
claims.source: Although Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent form of dementia, there are limited treatments to alleviate symptoms and none that halt its progression.
claims.evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claims.claim: There are limited treatments to alleviate AD symptoms and none that halt its progression.
claims.source: Although Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent form of dementia, there are limited treatments to alleviate symptoms and none that halt its progression.
claims.evidence: This reflects the current state of AD therapeutics as of the manuscript's writing.

claims.claim: Extracellular senile plaques of amyloid beta are histological features of AD.
claims.source: Histological features of AD are extracellular senile plaques of amyloid beta (Aβ) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of tau (Glenner et al., 1984; Goedert et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of tau are histological features of AD.
claims.source: Histological features of AD are extracellular senile plaques of amyloid beta (Aβ) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of tau (Glenner et al., 1984; Goedert et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Tau aggregation correlates better to disease progression than Aβ aggregation.
claims.source: While Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at the early stages of AD, tau aggregation correlates better to disease progression, with characteristic spreading along linked brain areas, and severity of symptoms correlating to the number of observed inclusions (Tanzi, 2012; Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Manczak and Reddy, 2014; Seward et al., 2013; Brier et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claims.claim: Tau pathology shows characteristic spreading along linked brain areas.
claims.source: While Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at the early stages of AD, tau aggregation correlates better to disease progression, with characteristic spreading along linked brain areas, and severity of symptoms correlating to the number of observed inclusions (Tanzi, 2012; Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Manczak and Reddy, 2014; Seward et al., 2013; Brier et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Severity of AD symptoms correlates to the number of observed tau inclusions.
claims.source: While Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at the early stages of AD, tau aggregation correlates better to disease progression, with characteristic spreading along linked brain areas, and severity of symptoms correlating to the number of observed inclusions (Tanzi, 2012; Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Manczak and Reddy, 2014; Seward et al., 2013; Brier et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Structural information about aggregated forms of Aβ and tau has not led to successful chemical interventions.
claims.source: Structural information about the aggregated forms of Aβ and tau is accumulating, but to date this knowledge has not led to successful chemical interventions (Chen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation and reflects the state of the field.

claims.claim: A link between Aβ and tau pathologies has been noted in transgenic mouse models.
claims.source: A link between the appearance of Aβ and tau pathologies has been noted in transgenic mouse models generated by crossing or co-expressing mutant Aβ and mutant tau, but the mechanism is not yet understood at the molecular level (Oddo et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The molecular mechanism linking Aβ and tau pathologies is not yet understood.
claims.source: A link between the appearance of Aβ and tau pathologies has been noted in transgenic mouse models generated by crossing or co-expressing mutant Aβ and mutant tau, but the mechanism is not yet understood at the molecular level (Oddo et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This statement reflects the knowledge gap the study aims to address.

claims.claim: Injecting Aβ seeds can induce tau pathology at the injection site and in functionally connected brain areas.
claims.source: By injecting Aβ seeds derived from synthetic peptide, transgenic mouse or AD patient tissue, tau pathology can be found both at the site of injection, and also in functionally connected brain areas (Bolmont et al., 2007; Götz et al., 2001; Morales et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Tau aggregation follows Aβ seeding in 3D neuronal stem cell cultures expressing early onset hereditary mutations.
claims.source: Tau aggregation has also been reported to follow Aβ seeding in 3D neuronal stem cell cultures that express early onset hereditary mutations to drive overproduction and aggregation of Aβ (Choi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The molecular linkage of Aβ to tau remains unresolved.
claims.source: In spite of these observations, the molecular linkage of Aβ to tau remains unresolved.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies the research gap.

claims.claim: One proposed hypothesis is that Aβ causes downstream cellular changes that trigger tau phosphorylation and eventual aggregation.
claims.source: Proposed hypotheses include Aβ causing downstream cellular changes that trigger tau phosphorylation and eventual aggregation, and/or a direct interaction and seeding of tau by aggregated Aβ (Ittner and Götz, 2011; Stancu et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This hypothesis is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: One proposed hypothesis is that there is a direct interaction and seeding of tau by aggregated Aβ.
claims.source: Proposed hypotheses include Aβ causing downstream cellular changes that trigger tau phosphorylation and eventual aggregation, and/or a direct interaction and seeding of tau by aggregated Aβ (Ittner and Götz, 2011; Stancu et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This hypothesis is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Aβ may be cleaved from APP inside endosomes and then exported.
claims.source: One possible model for intracellular aggregation could be that Aβ is cleaved from APP inside endosomes, and then exported (Rajendran et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Smaller diffusible Aβ oligomers are proposed to be the toxic species.
claims.source: Another model proposes that smaller diffusible Aβ oligomers are the toxic species (Lesné et al., 2006; Lambert et al., 1998; Benilova et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This is a widely discussed hypothesis supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Oligomers of Aβ isolated from AD serum are sufficient to induce tau aggregation.
claims.source: indeed oligomers of Aβ isolated from AD serum are sufficient to induce tau aggregation (Jin et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Aβ has been found to co-localize intra-neuronally with tau and at synaptic terminals.
claims.source: Aβ has also been found co-localize intra-neuronally with tau as well as at synaptic terminals, with increased interactions correlating with disease progression (Manczak and Reddy, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Increased Aβ-tau interactions correlate with disease progression.
claims.source: Aβ has also been found co-localize intra-neuronally with tau as well as at synaptic terminals, with increased interactions correlating with disease progression (Manczak and Reddy, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Soluble and insoluble complexes of Aβ bound to tau have been detected in AD tissue extracts.
claims.source: Furthermore, soluble and insoluble complexes of Aβ bound to tau have been detected in AD tissue extracts (Manczak and Reddy, 2014; Guo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Soluble complexes of Aβ and tau promote aggregation of tau in vitro.
claims.source: In vitro, soluble complexes of Aβ and tau have been found to promote aggregation of tau (Guo et al., 2006)
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Aβ fibrils can seed tau in vitro.
claims.source: while another study found that Aβ fibrils can seed tau (Vasconcelos et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Cross-seeding of tau by Aβ promotes tangle formation in AD.
claims.source: Taking the evidence together, we hypothesize that cross-seeding of tau by Aβ promotes tangle formation in AD, which could be prevented not only by inhibiting Aβ aggregation, but also by disrupting the binding site of Aβ with tau.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis based on cited evidence.

claims.claim: The amyloid core KLVFFA of Aβ binds tau.
claims.source: In Aβ, both the amyloid core KLVFFA, along with region spanning the carboxy terminal residues were found to bind tau (Guo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The carboxy terminal region of Aβ binds tau.
claims.source: In Aβ, both the amyloid core KLVFFA, along with region spanning the carboxy terminal residues were found to bind tau (Guo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Peptides from regions of tau in exons 7 and 9 bind Aβ.
claims.source: Conversely peptides from regions of tau in exons 7 and 9, well as aggregation prone sequences VQIINK and VQIVYK located at the beginning of repeat 2 (R2) and repeat 3 (R3) of the microtubule domain (K18), respectively, were found to bind Aβ (Guo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Tau sequences VQIINK and VQIVYK bind Aβ.
claims.source: Conversely peptides from regions of tau in exons 7 and 9, well as aggregation prone sequences VQIINK and VQIVYK located at the beginning of repeat 2 (R2) and repeat 3 (R3) of the microtubule domain (K18), respectively, were found to bind Aβ (Guo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: A computational seeding model predicts that the amyloid core of Aβ can form intermolecular β-sheet interactions with VQIINK or VQIVYK.
claims.source: A computational seeding model predicts that the amyloid core of Aβ can form intermolecular β-sheet interactions with VQIINK or VQIVYK (Miller et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The amyloid core segment is an important sequence for Aβ aggregation.
claims.source: On this basis, we hypothesized that an inhibitor capable of targeting the amyloid core, which itself is an important sequence for Aβ aggregation (Tjernberg et al., 1999; Bernstein et al., 2005; Marshall et al., 2016), might block both Aβ aggregation and tau seeding by Aβ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The amyloid core segment has been observed in multiple conformations in steric zipper structures.
claims.source: However, this segment has been observed in multiple conformations in steric zipper structures (Colletier et al., 2011) and fiber models (Lührs et al., 2005; Colvin et al., 2016; Qiang et al., 2012; Huber et al., 2015; Wälti et al., 2016), impeding structure-based inhibitor design.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The Iowa early onset hereditary mutation in Aβ is D23N.
claims.source: In an effort to characterize a toxic conformation of this sequence, we focused our efforts on determining the structure of the segment 16–26, containing the Iowa early onset hereditary mutation, D23N (Van Nostrand et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The designed inhibitors blocked aggregation of Aβ.
claims.source: Based on this structure, we designed several inhibitors and found that they indeed blocked aggregation of Aβ, prevented cross-seeding of tau by Aβ, and surprisingly, also blocked tau homotypic seeding.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the Results section.

claims.claim: The designed inhibitors prevented cross-seeding of tau by Aβ.
claims.source: Based on this structure, we designed several inhibitors and found that they indeed blocked aggregation of Aβ, prevented cross-seeding of tau by Aβ, and surprisingly, also blocked tau homotypic seeding.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the Results section.

claims.claim: The designed inhibitors blocked tau homotypic seeding.
claims.source: Based on this structure, we designed several inhibitors and found that they indeed blocked aggregation of Aβ, prevented cross-seeding of tau by Aβ, and surprisingly, also blocked tau homotypic seeding.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the Results section.

claims.claim: The efficacy of the inhibitors against both Aβ and tau implies a similar binding interface on both proteins.
claims.source: We suggest that the efficacy of these structure-based inhibitors against both proteins, but not other amyloid fibrils, implies there is a similar binding interface displayed on both Aβ and tau aggregates, supporting the cross-amyloid cascade hypothesis in AD.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing dual efficacy.

claims.claim: The inhibitors do not affect other amyloid fibrils.
claims.source: We suggest that the efficacy of these structure-based inhibitors against both proteins, but not other amyloid fibrils, implies there is a similar binding interface displayed on both Aβ and tau aggregates, supporting the cross-amyloid cascade hypothesis in AD.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with α-synuclein and hIAPP shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: Crystals of Aβ16-26 D23N used for MicroED were only a few hundred nanometers thick.
claims.source: With crystals only a few hundred nanometers thick, we used micro-electron diffraction (MicroED) to determine the structure of Aβ residues 16–26 containing the hereditary mutation D23N, (Figure 1A), KLVFFAENVGS.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N structure revealed pairs of anti-parallel β-sheets.
claims.source: The structure revealed pairs of anti-parallel β-sheets each composed of ~4000 strands, stacked into a fibril that spans the entire length of the crystal.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Each β-sheet in the Aβ16-26 D23N structure is composed of ~4000 strands.
claims.source: The structure revealed pairs of anti-parallel β-sheets each composed of ~4000 strands, stacked into a fibril that spans the entire length of the crystal.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claims.claim: Neighboring sheets in the Aβ16-26 D23N structure are oriented face to back, defining a Class seven steric zipper motif.
claims.source: Neighboring sheets are oriented face to back (Figure 1B, Table 1) defining a Class seven steric zipper motif.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The three C-terminal residues of Aβ16-26 D23N adopt an extended, non-β conformation.
claims.source: In addition, the three C-terminal residues adopt an extended, non-β conformation which stabilizes the packing between steric zippers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The sheet-sheet interface in Aβ16-26 D23N is strengthened by interdigitating side chains.
claims.source: The sheet–sheet interface is strengthened by interdigitating side chains, Lys 16, Val18, Phe20, Glu22 from the face of one strand, and Leu17, Phe19, and the N-terminus from the back of the other.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N zipper has a shape complementarity of 0.76.
claims.source: The zipper has an extensive interface with a high shape complementarity of 0.76 and a total buried solvent accessible surface area of 258 Å2.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N zipper has a total buried solvent accessible surface area of 258 Å2.
claims.source: The zipper has an extensive interface with a high shape complementarity of 0.76 and a total buried solvent accessible surface area of 258 Å2.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N structure is partly identical to the structure of Aβ16-21 (crystal form-I).
claims.source: This structure is partly identical to that of a shorter peptide segment, Aβ16–21, KLVFFA (crystal form-I) (Colletier et al., 2011), which we used successfully as a search model for molecular replacement.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison and successful molecular replacement.

claims.claim: Both Aβ16-26 D23N and Aβ16-21 have class seven symmetry.
claims.source: Both the longer and shorter segments have class seven symmetry.
claims.evidence: This is observed from structural analysis.

claims.claim: Aβ16-26 D23N and Aβ16-21 differ in registry.
claims.source: However, the two segments differ in registry.
claims.evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claims.claim: Aβ16-21 maintains an in-register hydrogen bonding pattern.
claims.source: The shorter segment maintains an in-register hydrogen bonding pattern while the longer segment is out-of-register.
claims.evidence: This is observed from structural analysis.

claims.claim: Aβ16-26 D23N is out-of-register.
claims.source: The shorter segment maintains an in-register hydrogen bonding pattern while the longer segment is out-of-register.
claims.evidence: This is observed from structural analysis.

claims.claim: The strands of Aβ16-26 D23N are tilted away from perpendicular to the fibril axis.
claims.source: That is, the strands of Aβ16–26 are tilted away from perpendicular to the fibril axis—a departure from canonical cross-β architecture.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The elongated beta strand from residues 16-22 has been observed in full length in vitro fibrillar structure determined by cryoEM.
claims.source: This elongated beta strand from residues 16–22 has also been observed in the full length in vitro fibrillar structure determined by cryoEM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Gremer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The antiparallel architecture and lack of registration of Aβ16-26 D23N suggest this assembly has characteristics of an amyloid oligomer.
claims.source: The antiparallel architecture and lack of registration of Aβ16–26 suggest this crystalline 'fibrillar'-like assembly has some characteristics of an amyloid oligomer.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural features and comparison with known oligomer structures.

claims.claim: Structural studies of amyloid oligomers most frequently reveal anti-parallel β sheet architecture.
claims.source: Structural studies of amyloid oligomers most frequently reveal anti-parallel β sheet architecture (Tay et al., 2013; Laganowsky et al., 2012; Sarkar et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Fibril structures have revealed parallel β sheets.
claims.source: whereas fibril structures have revealed parallel β sheets (Lührs et al., 2005; Colvin et al., 2016; Wälti et al., 2016; Krotee et al., 2018)
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Some short segments of Aβ show antiparallel β sheets.
claims.source: with the exception of some short segments of Aβ (Colletier et al., 2011) and in Aβ1-40 containing the early onset hereditary mutation D23N which leads to in-register anti-parallel fiber deposition in plaques (Qiang et al., 2012; Tycko et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Aβ1-40 containing D23N mutation leads to in-register anti-parallel fiber deposition in plaques.
claims.source: with the exception of some short segments of Aβ (Colletier et al., 2011) and in Aβ1-40 containing the early onset hereditary mutation D23N which leads to in-register anti-parallel fiber deposition in plaques (Qiang et al., 2012; Tycko et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Out-of-register stacking of anti-parallel β strands has been proposed to be the defining trait of toxic oligomers.
claims.source: The out-of-register stacking of anti-parallel β strands has been proposed to be the defining trait of toxic oligomers (Laganowsky et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Aβ16-22 has been proposed to form oligomers in silico.
claims.source: The segment Aβ16–22 has been proposed to be able to form such oligomers in silica (Sun et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The laboratory has developed a Rosetta-based design strategy using steric zipper structures to design capping peptide inhibitors.
claims.source: Our laboratory has developed a Rosetta-based design strategy using steric zipper structures to design capping peptide inhibitors for a number of amyloid proteins implicated in disease (Sievers et al., 2011; Seidler et al., 2018; Saelices et al., 2015; Soragni et al., 2016; Krotee et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references to previous work.

claims.claim: The structure was truncated to residues 16-22 for the search model.
claims.source: We chose to truncate our structure to residues 16–22 for the search model, omitting the residues not in the β strand.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological decision described in the text.

claims.claim: Six distinct inhibitor candidates were chosen from the first round of design.
claims.source: From our first round of design, we chose six distinct inhibitor candidates; those that were identified as good candidates but containing strong amino acid similarities to other top inhibitors were discarded.
claims.evidence: This describes the design process.

claims.claim: The initial pool of inhibitors contained four L-form peptides (L1-L4) and two D-peptides (D1 and D2).
claims.source: Our initial pool of inhibitors contained four L-form peptides, 2 each of 6 and 8 amino acids length, termed L1-L4, and two D-peptides six amino acids long, termed D1 and D2.
claims.evidence: This describes the initial inhibitor set.

claims.claim: Inhibitor efficacy was assessed at a 10 molar excess by testing prevention of Aβ1-42 toxicity on Neuro-2a cells.
claims.source: We assessed the efficacy of the inhibitors at a 10 molar excess by testing if they prevented Aβ1-42 toxicity on Neuro-2a (N2a) cells, a mouse neuroblastoma cell line, (Olmsted et al., 1970).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claims.claim: Cytotoxicity was measured using MTT dye reduction.
claims.source: We measured cytotoxicity using 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)−2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) dye reduction (Mosmann, 1983; Liu et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental method with citations.

claims.claim: Inhibitor D1 with sequence (D)-LYIWVQ eliminated the toxic effect of Aβ1-42.
claims.source: Our toxicity assay revealed one inhibitor, D1 with the sequence (D)-LYIWVQ, that was able to eliminate the toxic effect of Aβ1-42 (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the MTT assay shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: None of the inhibitors were toxic to N2a cells alone.
claims.source: none of the inhibitors were toxic to N2a cells alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: In the molecular model, smaller hydrophobic residues of D1 mimic interactions with the fibril interface.
claims.source: In our molecular model of the inhibitor, smaller hydrophobic residues of D1 mimic interactions with the fibril interface on one side of the peptide, which promotes recognition, (Figure 2B)
claims.evidence: This is shown in the molecular model in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Large aromatic residues on the other side of D1 block possible further interactions.
claims.source: while the other side of the peptide positions large aromatic residues between Aβ residues, blocking possible further interactions (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the molecular model in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Six new inhibitor designs were selected and tested in the second round of design.
claims.source: We selected and tested six new designs.
claims.evidence: This describes the design process.

claims.claim: Four second-generation inhibitors were eight amino acids long (D1a-D1d).
claims.source: Of the six, four were eight amino acids long such that the inhibitor would extend over more of our crystal structure, which we called D1a-D1d.
claims.evidence: This describes the inhibitor design.

claims.claim: Two second-generation inhibitors (D1e and D1f) were six amino acids long with slight sequence perturbations from D1.
claims.source: The additional two, termed D1e and D1f, were six amino acids long featuring slight sequence perturbations from D1 (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the inhibitor design.

claims.claim: Inhibitors D1b and D1d were effective at reducing Aβ1-42 toxicity at both tenfold excess and equimolar ratio.
claims.source: We identified two of the eight amino acid long inhibitors, D1b and D1d, that were also effective at reducing AB1-42 toxicity at both a tenfold excess and at an equimolar ratio (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: All tested inhibitors (D1, D1b, D1d) elicited a dose-dependent response with estimated IC50 of less than 1 μM.
claims.source: We found that all inhibitors elicited a dose dependent response, with all having an estimated IC50 of less than 1 μM.
claims.evidence: This is based on dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The cognate negative peptide control LC (L-form of D1) did not reduce toxicity.
claims.source: The cognate negative peptide control, LC, the L-form peptide of inhibitor D1, did not reduce toxicity (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: All inhibitors reduce fibril formation in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: We observe that all of our inhibitors reduce fibril formation in a dose dependent manner, while the negative control peptide, LC, does not (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown by ThT assays in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The longer inhibitors D1b and D1d appear effective at an equimolar ratio.
claims.source: The longer inhibitors, D1b and D1d, appear effective at an equimolar ratio.
claims.evidence: This is observed in ThT assays shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: At higher concentrations, the inhibitors appear to self-assemble but remain effective at reducing Aβ1-42 toxicity.
claims.source: However, when assayed at higher concentrations, the inhibitors appear to self-assemble, but remain effective at reducing Aβ1-42 toxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2E.

claims.claim: TEM analysis confirmed the reduced abundance of Aβ1-42 fibrils after 72 hr.
claims.source: After 72 hr, samples were taken for negative-stain TEM analysis, which confirmed the reduced abundance of Aβ1–42 fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is shown by TEM images in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: D1b and D1d were more effective at reducing fibril formation than D1.
claims.source: D1b and D1d were more effective at reducing fibril formation than D1, although all three inhibitors showed near equal efficiency in reducing toxicity.
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing ThT and TEM data in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Fibrils were observed in the equimolar ratio sample of Aβ1-42 with D1, but not with D1b and D1d.
claims.source: Fibrils were observed in the equimolar ratio sample of Aβ1-42 with D1, whereas the comparable samples with D1b and D1d did not contain fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is shown by TEM images in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Inhibitors D1a and D1c were less effective at blocking fiber formation.
claims.source: Inhibitors that were not efficient at preventing toxicity, such as D1a and D1c, were also less effective at blocking fiber formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: All inhibitors reduced the formation of Aβ1-42 assemblies recognized by conformational monoclonal antibodies.
claims.source: We used conformational antibodies to probe samples of Aβ1-42 incubated with a 10-molar excess of inhibitor overnight at 37°C. Binding by oligomer specific conformational antibody A11 and A11-O9, a monoclonal variant of A11, was reduced by all of our inhibitors (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is shown by dot blot assays in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The inhibitors reduced the abundance of Aβ conformations recognized by antibodies mOC24, mOC64, mOC104, and mOC116.
claims.source: Additionally, the inhibitors reduced the abundance of Aβ conformations recognized by antibodies mOC24, mOC64, mOC104, and mOC116.
claims.evidence: This is shown by dot blot assays in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Antibodies mOC24, mOC64, mOC104, and mOC116 bind fibrillar plaques from patient-derived AD tissue and/or 3xTg-AD mouse tissue.
claims.source: These antibodies bind fibrillar plaques from patient derived AD tissue and/or 3xTg-AD mouse tissue (Hatami et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Adding inhibitor to monomeric Aβ1-42 prior to incubation had a marked difference from adding inhibitor to pre-formed Aβ1-42 oligomers.
claims.source: We found that adding the inhibitor to monomeric Aβ1-42 prior to incubation had a marked difference from adding inhibitor to pre-formed Aβ1-42 oligomers.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing experiments in Figure 2E and Figure 4A.

claims.claim: When co-incubated with monomeric Aβ, D1 was as effective as D1b and D1d at reducing toxicity.
claims.source: When co-incubated with monomeric Aβ, the shorter D1 inhibitor was as effective as D1b and D1d at reducing toxicity
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: When added to pre-formed Aβ assemblies, only the longer inhibitors D1b and D1d were effective at reducing toxicity.
claims.source: however, when added to pre-formed Aβ assemblies, only the longer inhibitors D1b and D1d were effective at reducing toxicity (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Both D1b and D1d could fully ameliorate toxicity of aggregates at 10 μM.

results.result: The crystal structure of Aβ16-26 D23N was determined by MicroED, revealing pairs of anti-parallel β-sheets with ~4000 strands each, arranged in a Class seven steric zipper motif with face-to-back orientation. The structure shows out-of-register stacking with strands tilted from perpendicular to the fibril axis, and shares partial identity with the shorter Aβ16-21 segment but differs in registry.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C49-C63 provide comprehensive structural characterization supported by crystallographic data (Table 1), electron microscopy (Figure 1A), and structural analysis (Figure 1B). The MicroED methodology is appropriate for nanometer-thick crystals, and the structural features are well-documented with quantitative metrics (shape complementarity 0.76, buried surface area 258 Å²). The comparison with known structures (C57, C63) provides validation.

results.result: The Aβ16-26 D23N structure exhibits characteristics of both fibrillar and oligomeric assemblies, with antiparallel architecture and out-of-register stacking suggesting oligomer-like features, while the extended β-strand resembles fibrillar structures. This dual nature is supported by comparison with literature showing oligomers typically display antiparallel β-sheets while fibrils show parallel arrangements.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are well-supported by structural analysis and extensive literature citations. The inference that the structure has oligomeric characteristics (C64) is justified by the antiparallel, out-of-register architecture, which is documented as a defining trait of toxic oligomers (C69). The comparison with known oligomer and fibril structures from multiple cited studies provides strong support.

results.result: Structure-based inhibitor design using Rosetta identified D1 (D-LYIWVQ) as an effective inhibitor that eliminated Aβ1-42 toxicity in N2a cells at 10-fold molar excess. The molecular model shows D1 mimics fibril interface interactions on one side while positioning large aromatic residues to block further interactions on the other side. Second-generation inhibitors D1b and D1d (8 amino acids) were also identified as effective.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C83 describe a systematic inhibitor design and screening process supported by MTT toxicity assays (Figure 2A), molecular modeling (Figure 2B,C), and dose-response data. The methodology is clearly described, controls are appropriate (LC negative control, C78), and the structure-function relationship is well-rationalized through molecular modeling (C79-C80). The iterative design process is logical and well-documented.

results.result: Inhibitors D1, D1b, and D1d showed dose-dependent reduction of Aβ1-42 toxicity with IC50 values less than 1 μM, while the L-form control peptide LC showed no effect. D1b and D1d were effective at both tenfold excess and equimolar ratios.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by dose-response curves (Figure 2E) and supplementary data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C). The statistical analysis appears appropriate with ANOVA testing, and the negative control (LC) validates specificity. The IC50 estimation methodology is standard, though the exact fitting parameters are not fully detailed.

results.result: All inhibitors reduced Aβ1-42 fibril formation in a dose-dependent manner as measured by ThT fluorescence, with D1b and D1d being more effective than D1 at equimolar ratios. TEM analysis confirmed reduced fibril abundance after 72 hours. At higher concentrations, inhibitors self-assembled but remained effective at reducing toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 are well-supported by complementary ThT assays (Figure 3A) and TEM imaging (Figure 3B). The dose-dependent effects are clearly demonstrated, and the correlation between fibril reduction and toxicity reduction strengthens the mechanistic interpretation. The observation of inhibitor self-assembly (C89) is appropriately noted as a caveat, though it doesn't compromise the main findings.

results.result: Inhibitors reduced the formation of Aβ1-42 assemblies recognized by conformational antibodies including oligomer-specific A11/A11-O9 and fibril-binding antibodies mOC24, mOC64, mOC104, and mOC116 that recognize disease-relevant conformations from AD patient tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are supported by dot blot assays (Figure 3C, supplementary figures) using well-characterized conformational antibodies. The use of multiple antibodies recognizing different epitopes strengthens the conclusion that inhibitors affect multiple toxic species. The antibody characterization is supported by citation (C96), though independent validation of antibody specificity in this system would strengthen the claims.

results.result: Inhibitor efficacy differed between preventing aggregation of monomeric Aβ versus reducing toxicity of pre-formed aggregates. D1 was as effective as D1b/D1d against monomeric Aβ, but only D1b and D1d reduced toxicity of pre-formed aggregates, with D1d being more potent (effective to 1 μM). The difference between D1b and D1d is attributed to residue 6 (Gln vs Trp).
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C105 are supported by comparing experiments in Figures 2E and 4A, showing clear differential efficacy. The structure-activity relationship inference (C103) is reasonable based on sequence comparison (C102) and efficacy data, though direct mutagenesis experiments would provide stronger support. The general conclusion about differential sensitivity (C105) is well-supported by the data pattern.

results.result: Inhibitors do not disaggregate Aβ fibers but rather cap or coat them at toxicity-inducing interfaces, as shown by TEM imaging of fibers remaining after inhibitor treatment. SPR measurements showed D1d binds Aβ1-42 fibrils with an apparent Kd of 52 μM, though the true Kd may be lower due to D1d self-interaction and fibril polymorphism.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 are supported by TEM (Figure 4B) and SPR data (Figure 4C). The capping mechanism (C107) is a reasonable inference from the TEM observations and inhibitor design, though direct structural evidence of capping would strengthen this claim. The SPR analysis is appropriate, and the authors appropriately note caveats about the Kd measurement (C109) due to experimental complications.

results.result: Aβ fibrils (both Aβ1-42 and Aβ16-26 D23N) seeded tau K18+ aggregation in vitro, though less efficiently than K18 self-seeding. This seeding was also observed with full-length tau in the presence of heparin. Conversely, K18 could not seed Aβ aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 are supported by ThT assays (Figure 5A, supplementary figures) showing clear seeding effects. The unidirectional seeding (Aβ→tau but not tau→Aβ) is an important observation. The experiments use appropriate controls and the methodology is standard for seeding assays. The lower efficiency of Aβ seeding compared to tau self-seeding is appropriately noted.

results.result: Aβ fibrils induced intracellular tau aggregates in tau-K18 biosensor cells at approximately 2.5% the efficiency of tau40 seeds. Other amyloid protein fibrils (α-synuclein, hIAPP) and non-fibrillar Aβ were not seeding-competent in this system, demonstrating specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116 are supported by biosensor cell assays (Figure 5B, supplementary figures) with appropriate statistical analysis. The low efficiency of Aβ seeding (2.5%) is appropriately acknowledged and discussed. The specificity controls (C116) are important and well-executed, showing the system can discriminate between different amyloid structures.

results.result: All inhibitors reduced Aβ-mediated tau seeding at 20 μM, with D1b showing reduction at concentrations as low as 1 μM. D1d was more effective at inhibiting Aβ toxicity, while D1b was more effective at reducing tau seeding, demonstrating differential efficacy profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 are supported by biosensor cell assays (Figure 5D,E) with clear dose-response relationships and statistical analysis. The differential efficacy between D1b and D1d (C119-C120) is an important finding supported by comparing data from Figures 4A and 5D. This suggests different structural requirements for blocking toxicity versus seeding.

results.result: Mutagenesis of the Aβ steric zipper interface showed that residues K16, V18, and E22 are critical for tau seeding. Aβ1-42 K16A/V18A/E22A fibrils did not seed tau, while L17R/F19R fibrils seeded similarly to wild-type and were inhibited by D1b.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by mutagenesis experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) that directly test the seeding interface. The experimental design is logical, and the results clearly identify critical residues. The inference about the seeding interface (C124) is well-supported by the mutagenesis pattern, though additional mutations would further validate the interface definition.

results.result: Inhibitors D1, D1b, and D1d reduced tau40 aggregation in a dose-dependent manner, while control LC did not. The inhibitors did not block aggregation of α-synuclein or hIAPP, demonstrating specificity for Aβ and tau rather than general anti-amyloid activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 are supported by ThT assays with tau40 (Figure 6A) and specificity controls with other amyloid proteins (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). The specificity experiments (C127-C128) are crucial for establishing that these are not general amyloid inhibitors. The negative control (LC) validates the D-amino acid requirement.

results.result: D1b was the most effective inhibitor of tau40 fibril seeding with an IC50 of 4.5 μM, while D1 showed slight effectiveness and D1d required 75 μM for seeding reduction in biosensor cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 are supported by dose-response data in biosensor cells (Figure 6B,C). The IC50 calculation for D1b appears appropriate, and the differential efficacy among inhibitors is clearly demonstrated. The pattern differs from Aβ inhibition, suggesting different structural requirements for tau versus Aβ.

results.result: D1b most effectively inhibited seeding by tau mutants with intact VQIINK interface A (I277), solvent-accessible VQIVYK interface, and 3R tau. A tau40 mutant with all interfaces disrupted did not seed, indicating at least one interface is required. Both VQIINK and VQIVYK segments are inhibited by D1b and may share structural features with the Aβ core.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C137 are supported by systematic mutagenesis experiments (Figure 6D, supplementary figures) testing different tau interfaces. The experimental design is comprehensive, testing multiple interface mutants. The null mutant control (C133-C134) is important for validating that known interfaces are required for seeding. The inference about shared structural features (C137) is reasonable but would benefit from direct structural evidence.

results.result: D1b significantly reduced seeding by brain-derived lysates from all tested AD brain regions (hippocampus, frontal cortex, occipital lobe) and PSP tauopathy tissue. The efficacy against both AD and PSP suggests D1b recognizes a common toxic epitope in multiple tau polymorphs.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 are supported by experiments with human brain tissue (Figure 7) showing significant reduction in seeding. The inclusion of PSP tissue (which lacks Aβ) is particularly important for demonstrating tau-specific effects. Statistical analysis shows significance, though the variable seeding efficiency across tissues (noted by authors) is appropriately acknowledged. The inference about a common epitope (C140) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: Structural overlay of the Aβ16-26 segment with tau R2 (VQIINK) and R3 (VQIVYK) regions reveals high backbone similarity and complementary sidechain interdigitation. Aβ overlays well with tau in both parallel and antiparallel orientations, suggesting the amyloid core and these tau regions can form similar structures capable of cross-seeding.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143 are supported by structural overlays (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) showing low RMSD values (0.53-0.56 Å). The computational modeling is appropriate, though the energy minimization using Foldit should be validated with more rigorous methods. The inference about cross-seeding capability (C143) is reasonable based on structural similarity but remains somewhat speculative without direct structural evidence of the cross-seeded complex.

results.result: D1b effectively reduced seeding from brain homogenates, while D1 and D1d were much less effective. The tau mutagenesis results suggest D1b can recognize at least two unique core interfaces of tau, potentially enabling activity against multiple tau strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C146 are supported by brain lysate experiments (Figure 7) and tau mutagenesis data (Figure 6D). The differential efficacy of inhibitors on patient-derived material is important for translational relevance. The inference about multiple interface recognition (C146) is well-supported by the mutagenesis experiments showing D1b inhibits both VQIINK and VQIVYK interfaces.

results.result: The dual efficacy of inhibitors against both Aβ and tau suggests these proteins share a common epitope, supporting the hypothesis that cross-seeding is a mechanism linking Aβ to tau aggregation. The results suggest direct interaction between the Aβ core and amyloid-prone tau regions facilitates cross-seeding, and controlling aggregation of both proteins may be necessary for treating AD.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C11, C47, C149-C151 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental data. The cross-seeding hypothesis is well-supported by: (1) Aβ seeding tau in vitro and in cells, (2) inhibitors blocking both Aβ and tau aggregation/seeding, (3) structural similarity between Aβ and tau segments, and (4) mutagenesis identifying critical interfaces. However, the therapeutic implication (C151) is somewhat speculative and would require in vivo validation.

results.result: The introduction establishes the background on AD pathology, the relationship between Aβ and tau, evidence for cross-seeding from prior studies, and the rationale for targeting the Aβ amyloid core. This includes the Iowa D23N mutation and known interaction sites between Aβ and tau.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C43 provide background context supported by extensive literature citations. These are primarily review of established knowledge and prior work rather than new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the synthesis of prior work provides good rationale for the study. However, as these are not original findings from this manuscript, they represent supporting context rather than primary results.

results.result: The designed inhibitors blocked Aβ aggregation, prevented Aβ-mediated tau cross-seeding, and blocked tau homotypic seeding, but did not affect other amyloid fibrils (α-synuclein, hIAPP).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46, C48 summarize key findings that are detailed in other result groups. These are high-level summary statements supported by the comprehensive experimental data described in other results. The specificity claim (C48) is particularly important and well-supported by negative controls with other amyloid proteins.

results.result: The Aβ16-26 D23N structure contains characteristics of both fibrillar and oligomeric structure.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 is a summary statement supported by detailed structural analysis in claims C64-C70. The dual nature is evidenced by antiparallel, out-of-register architecture (oligomer-like) combined with extended β-strands (fibril-like). This is a key structural finding that motivated the inhibitor design strategy.

results.result: Structure-based peptide inhibitors reduce Aβ aggregation and toxicity of already-aggregated species.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 are high-level summaries of findings detailed in other result groups (C87-C93 for aggregation, C97-C109 for pre-formed aggregates). Both claims are well-supported by ThT assays, TEM, and toxicity assays. These represent major functional outcomes of the inhibitor design.

results.result: The designed inhibitors reduce Aβ-mediated tau aggregation and reduce aggregation and self-seeding of tau fibrils.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 summarize findings detailed in other result groups (C110-C120 for cross-seeding, C125-C137 for tau homotypic seeding). Both claims are well-supported by in vitro ThT assays and biosensor cell experiments. These are major findings demonstrating the dual efficacy of the inhibitors.

results.result: The effective dose to reduce toxicity of aggregated species is higher than to delay aggregation of monomeric species. Inhibitors preventing aggregation nucleation are more promiscuous than those ameliorating toxicity by binding distinct structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C148 represent general conclusions about inhibitor mechanisms drawn from comparing multiple experiments. C147 is directly supported by data comparing Figures 2E and 4A. C148 is a reasonable inference from the differential efficacy patterns observed across inhibitors, though it is somewhat speculative as a general principle.
